023.subtitle: Lotus forest, kadamba grove, sea of nectar — and then her eyes

commentary.meaning: The previous verse moved steadily inward, from the world-mountain to the couch at the centre. This one reverses the direction and pulls back out. First a forest of lotuses, then a grove of kadamba trees, then the whole ocean of nectar in whose middle the island stands — each name a wider frame than the one before, until the field of view contains everything. And then, without warning, the hymn abandons geography altogether. The fourth name is two words long and concerns her eyes; the fifth says that she gives people what they want. After seven consecutive names of location, three in the preceding verse and four here counting the couch, the shift is abrupt and clearly deliberate. The metre marks it: the first three names each fill exactly one quarter-line, and then the last quarter is divided between two short names, so the pace changes audibly at the same moment the subject does. Having established that she lives at the centre of an elaborate world, the verse ends by saying that what matters about her is a look and a gift.
commentary.history:
The two versions of where she lives do not agree, and it is worth being clear about that rather than harmonising them. The previous verse put her on the middle summit of Meru; this one puts her on an island in a sea of nectar. Both are old and both are current, and practitioners hold them simultaneously without embarrassment. The island version has its own literature: the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa devotes a long passage to Maṇidvīpa, the island of jewels, and the Saundaryalaharī's eighth verse places her on an island in the sea of nectar. What is common to the two accounts is not the topography but the structure — a centre, approached across a distance, surrounded by increasingly precious enclosures.

Aṭavī, in the first name, is not the polite word for a garden. It means a forest or wilderness, a place one roams in and can be lost in, and pairing it with lotuses produces a strange image: flowers growing as thick and as tall as trees, so that a lotus bed becomes a landscape one enters. Commentators who read Śrīpura as a description of the subtle body rather than of a place take the great lotus forest as the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown of the head, and once that reading is admitted the rest of the geography follows it inward. The two readings are not alternatives to decide between; the external and internal versions of the map are meant to be laid over each other.

The kadamba is a real tree, common across the Indian plains, with dense spherical orange flower-heads that open at the first rains and carry a heavy scent. In poetry its flowering signals the monsoon's arrival, and it belongs to Kṛṣṇa's landscape in Vaiṣṇava literature as much as to the goddess's in Śākta. For this hymn it has a geography attached: Madurai is called Kadambavana in its own temple tradition, and Mīnākṣī who presides there is addressed as the dweller in the kadamba grove. The Saundaryalaharī plants kadamba around the house of wish-granting stone, using the tree's other Sanskrit name, nīpa. So the name has a double reference, to a grove in the mythical city and to an actual temple town in Tamil country, and readers of this hymn in the South have generally heard both.

Sudhā is the drink that makes the gods deathless, the same substance as amṛta, and the ocean of it recalls the most-told episode in Purāṇic literature. Gods and demons, having agreed to cooperate, used Mount Mandara as a churning-stick and the serpent Vāsuki as the rope, and turned the ocean until it yielded its treasures: Dhanvantari with the pot of nectar, the goddess Śrī, the wish-granting cow, the moon, the horse and elephant of the gods — and, before any of them, the poison Hālāhala, which Śiva swallowed and held in his throat, turning it blue. The story establishes what a sea of nectar is: not a decorative pool but the source of deathlessness, obtained only by prolonged and dangerous labour. In the internalised reading the nectar is the flow that descends from the crown when the ascending energy reaches it, and several later names in this hymn use the same vocabulary.

Then the verse turns. Kāmākṣī is a proper name before it is a description — the goddess of Kāñcīpuram, one of three great seats of goddess worship whose presiding deities are all named for their eyes: Kāmākṣī at Kāñcī, Mīnākṣī at Madurai, Viśālākṣī at Vārāṇasī. Since the kadamba name has just gestured at Madurai, the hymn is naming two of the three in adjacent breaths. At Kāñcī the local tradition offers a playful analysis, taking kā as Sarasvatī and ā as Lakṣmī, so that the two great goddesses are her two eyes; the straightforward reading is the one the grammar gives, that desire is in her eyes. Either way the register changes from architecture to face, and the tradition's long preoccupation with her sidelong glance, the kaṭākṣa that a petitioner actually hopes for, begins here.

Kāmadāyinī completes the turn. Kāma is one of the four recognised aims of human life, alongside dharma, wealth and liberation, and orthodox Indian ethics treats it not as illegitimate but as one good among others that must be kept in place. Śrīvidyā goes further than most schools in refusing to choose: it promises bhukti and mukti together, enjoyment and release, and treats the demand that a practitioner give up the first to obtain the second as a failure of nerve. A name saying plainly that she gives people what they want, placed immediately after a name about her eyes, is that position stated in the hymn's own idiom.
commentary.practice:
The verse divides into two unequal halves for the reciter: three long names of eight syllables each, filling three quarter-lines exactly, then a fourth quarter shared between kāmākṣī and kāmadāyinī. The change of pace is the point and should not be smoothed away. Come off the long names cleanly and let the two short ones stand separately; run together they sound like one word, and beginners regularly produce kāmākṣīkāmadāyinī with no join audible.

Mahāpadmāṭavīsaṃsthā contains three things worth isolating. The cluster dm in padma is dental d followed by labial m, both fully pronounced, with no vowel between. The ṭ of aṭavī is retroflex, made with the tongue tip curled back, and must not become the dental t that an English speaker's t naturally is. And saṃsthā carries an anusvāra before a sibilant, which here is not a consonant but a nasalisation of the preceding vowel: a nasalised sa flowing straight into sthā, not sam followed by a fresh syllable.

The cluster sth returns twice here, in saṃsthā and in sudhāsāgaramadhyasthā, having appeared three times in the verse before. Dental s, then aspirated dental th, one puff of breath.

Kadambavanavāsinī is the easiest name in the verse. The mb of kadamba is a labial nasal into a labial stop, exactly as in English "amber", and the rest is open syllables. Use it to recover breath control after the first name.

Sudhāsāgaramadhyasthā has two aspirated dentals, the dh of sudhā and the dh of madhya, and they must be distinguished from the unaspirated d of kadamba just behind them. Aspirated dh is voiced with a following breath — not d plus a separate h, and not the th of English "the". The cluster dhy in madhya is that aspirated dental releasing into the palatal glide.

Kāmākṣī turns on kṣ, the most distinctive conjunct in Sanskrit: guttural k followed by the retroflex sibilant ṣ, one unit, the tongue moving from soft palate to curled-back position within it. The common error is to substitute the sound in English "action", which palatalises the sibilant.

For the recitation done as archanā, this verse alternates its endings. The two names in -sthā are feminine ā-stems and take -āyai: mahāpadmāṭavīsaṃsthāyai namaḥ, sudhāsāgaramadhyasthāyai namaḥ. The other three are ī-stems and take -yai: kadambavanavāsinyai namaḥ, kāmākṣyai namaḥ, kāmadāyinyai namaḥ. The safe method is to identify the stem before reaching for the ending rather than to memorise the five forms.

What the verse asks is a change of attention halfway through. The first three names continue the work of the preceding verse, building a place; the last two stop building and look at somebody. A reciter who chants all five in the same manner has missed what the verse does. It is customary to let the two kāma names carry a different weight — quieter, and addressed rather than described — since after all the ramparts and oceans the hymn has arrived at the only two facts a petitioner needs, which are that she is looking and that she gives.

crossReferences.deva: बलं बलवतां चाहं कामरागविवर्जितम् । धर्माविरुद्धो भूतेषु कामोऽस्मि भरतर्षभ ॥
crossReferences.iast: balaṃ balavatāṃ cāhaṃ kāmarāgavivarjitam | dharmāviruddho bhūteṣu kāmo'smi bharatarṣabha ||
crossReferences.translation: I am the strength of the strong, free of desire and attachment; and in living beings I am that desire which is not in conflict with dharma, best of the Bharatas.
crossReferences.relevance: The orthodox frame within which kāmadāyinī is not a scandalous name. The Gītā does not condemn desire as such; it identifies itself with desire that keeps within bounds, which gives a broadly acceptable Vedāntic warrant for a goddess who hands people what they ask for. What Śrīvidyā adds is a refusal to treat the granting of desires as a lower concession made to weak practitioners, and the hymn's placement of this name beside her eyes rather than in a list of boons is part of that refusal.

crossReferences.deva: शिवे शृङ्गारार्द्रा तदितरजने कुत्सनपरा सरोषा गङ्गायां गिरिशचरिते विस्मयवती । हराहिभ्यो भीता सरसिरुहसौभाग्यजयिनी सखीषु स्मेरा ते मयि जननि दृष्टिः सकरुणा ॥
crossReferences.iast: śive śṛṅgārārdrā tad-itara-jane kutsanaparā saroṣā gaṅgāyāṃ giriśacarite vismayavatī | harāhibhyo bhītā sarasiruhasaubhāgyajayinī sakhīṣu smerā te mayi janani dṛṣṭiḥ sakaruṇā ||
crossReferences.translation: Toward Śiva, wet with love; toward anyone else, full of scorn; angry at the Ganges; astonished at the deeds of the lord of the mountain; frightened of Hara's snakes; outdoing the lotus in loveliness; smiling among her friends — and toward me, mother, your glance is compassionate.
crossReferences.relevance: An unfolding of kāmākṣī into eight simultaneous expressions. The first word of the verse, śṛṅgārārdrā, is the erotic sentiment made literally moist, and it is aimed at Śiva alone; the last word is the one that concerns the person praying. Read beside the sahasranāma's two-word name, it shows what the tradition thinks is packed into an eye: not one emotion but a whole set held at once, sorted by whom she is looking at.

references.title: The Mahābhārata, Volume 1: Book 1, The Book of the Beginning
references.author: tr. J. A. B. van Buitenen (University of Chicago Press, 1973)
references.note: The churning of the ocean is told in the first book, and van Buitenen's translation is the one to read it in — fast, unfussy, and free of the devotional padding that later retellings add. It is worth reading the episode whole rather than in summary, because the poison comes out before the nectar does, and that order is the point of the story.

references.title: The Sacred Marriage of a Hindu Goddess
references.author: William P. Harman (Indiana University Press, 1989)
references.note: A study of Mīnākṣī and the Madurai temple, which is what kadambavanavāsinī points at for most South Indian reciters. Harman is good on how a local goddess with her own myth gets absorbed into pan-Indian frameworks without losing her particularity, which is exactly the process this name records.

references.title: The Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam
references.author: tr. Swami Vijnanananda (Sacred Books of the Hindus; widely reprinted)
references.note: Contains the long description of Maṇidvīpa, the island in the sea of nectar, which is the fullest treatment of the geography behind the third name. The translation is Victorian and heavy going, but the passage is worth the effort for the sheer accumulation of detail, which shows that these descriptions were meant to be dwelt in rather than skimmed.

references.title: Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition
references.author: David Kinsley (University of California Press, 1986)
references.note: The standard survey, and the place to get oriented before deciding what Kāmākṣī, Mīnākṣī and Viśālākṣī have to do with one another. Kinsley is careful about the difference between a goddess's textual career and her local cult, which matters for a name that is simultaneously a common adjective and the proper name of a specific temple deity.

references.title: Devī: Goddesses of India
references.author: ed. John Stratton Hawley and Donna Marie Wulff (University of California Press, 1996)
references.note: A collection of essays rather than a single argument, and useful here because several contributors deal with South Indian goddesses and with the question of what worshippers actually ask for. Read it against kāmadāyinī: the essays make clear how much ordinary petitionary religion sits underneath the philosophical superstructure this hymn also carries.
